title: Aloud or silent
hookLine: reading aloud lets the sound work; reading silently helps focus
tomorrow: can a whole family read one book, one page each?

lines: ONE WORD, AGAIN AND AGAIN: SUNIAI.
cards: Some friends only send voice notes. Others would rather type a whole paragraph than hear their own voice played back. Reading the Guru's words splits people the same way: out loud, or in your head?
Here's an odd detail that helps. Early in the Japji, Guru Nanak lands on one word and won't let it go: suniai, by listening. Pauri after pauri, line after line opens with it.
Not by reading. By listening. Why would the opening of a book praise the ear?

teach.b: Start with what the lines promise. By listening, in paraphrase, come the wise and the devoted; by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away. And one line in the original: suniai andhe paavahi raahu.
By listening, even the blind find the road. Why the ear? Look at the rest of the book.
Its hymns sit under raga headings, the musical moods they're set in.

teach.h: HYMNS MADE TO BE SUNG AND HEARD.
teach.b: They were made to be sung and heard, not only seen. Something to tell someone tonight: the Japji spends pauri after pauri on listening before it turns to understanding.
So reading aloud lets your own ear hear the Guru's words, and the sound does its work even before the meaning arrives. Then the Japji turns.
The next run of pauris opens on mannai: by accepting, by taking it in. That's where quiet helps.

teach.h: ALOUD FOR SOUND, SILENT TO SETTLE.
teach.b: A slower, silent read lets one line settle and gives the mind something to hold. So the puzzle answers itself. The Japji's own order is hear it, then take it in.
Not aloud or silent. Aloud, then silent.

how: Sikhs read Gurbani aloud in the gurdwara and at home, and also sing it in kirtan; many also read a line again quietly, or with a translation beside it, to take in its meaning.

o: two ways to read Gurbani: for the ear, and to let it settle
a rule about which prayers are read aloud and which are not
a debate over whether silent prayer is allowed in a gurdwara

games.q: the Japji's order — tap the pairs.
p: hymns made to be sung and heard

s: it means by listening: the Japji praises the ear first.
the Granth's hymns were written as silent poems for the page
they sit under raga headings, the musical moods they're set in: made to be sung and heard.
in the Japji, the listening pauris come before the pauris on taking it in
first suniai, by listening; then mannai, by accepting.

games.q: your friend is studying for a test on the bus and wants to read a hymn on her phone, but she can't read aloud there. what does today's lesson suggest?
o: skip it; Gurbani only counts when it's read out loud.
read it silently now, and hear it aloud, or sung, when she can.
read it silently from now on, since meaning is what matters.
games.why: the Japji's order is hear it, then take it in. the quiet read lets a line settle; the sound, when it comes, does its own work.

practice: Choose one line you know, from the Japji, a gutka, or simply the opening words if those are what's in your ear. Say it aloud once, slowly, and listen to your own voice carry it.
Then read or say it again in silence, and stay with whatever each way gave you.

wordCard.voice: Aloud or silent. Two ways to meet the Guru's words: the sound in the ear, and the meaning settling in. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: suniai, by listening; the word that opens line after line in the Japji's listening pauris.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: aloud and silent, first for the ear, then for the heart. Until tomorrow.
